lead.headline: Voyager 1's Messages Now Take a Whole Day
lead.deck: The old space probe is one light-day from Earth. Here is how a radio call works that far away.
body: Imagine waiting a whole day for your words to reach a friend. That is what talking to Voyager 1 is like now. Voyager 1 is a probe, a robot spacecraft. On 18 November it reached one light-day from Earth.
A light-day is a distance. It is how far light travels in 24 hours, about 16.1 billion miles. No human-made object has gone farther.

Engineers talk to the probe with radio waves, which move at the speed of light. So a message from Earth now takes 24 hours to reach the probe. Its answer takes another 24 hours to come back. So engineers wait two whole days for each answer.
Since 14 November, no science data has come back. But Voyager 1, launched in 1977, still sends a steady radio tone. Engineers used that tone to confirm the light-day mark.

science.headline: Lost Meerkats Make a Beeline for Home
science.deck: A new study shows that a meerkat on its own can find its way back to its group.
body: Meerkats are small, furry animals that live in groups of up to 50. Scientists at the University of Zurich, in Switzerland, wondered: can one meerkat find its way home alone?

To find out, they worked in the Kalahari Desert in southern Africa. They fitted meerkats with GPS collars, which track where an animal goes. Then they moved each meerkat 1.5 kilometres from its group, longer than 15 football fields, and let it go.
They did this 20 times. In 18 of the 20 tries, the meerkat made a beeline, a straight path, back to its group or the spot where it was caught.
How? Each meerkat stood up on its back legs to scan the land. Then it set off in a straight line. Now and then it paused to look around or sniff for smells it knew.
Even young meerkats got home. The scientists think meerkats may form a mental map, a picture of home kept in the brain, early in life.

world.headline: Eritrea Gets Rid of an Eye Disease Called Trachoma
world.deck: World health experts say the East African country has stopped trachoma being a public health problem.
body: Eritrea is a country in East Africa. On 16 November the World Health Organization, or WHO, said Eritrea has eliminated trachoma as a public health problem. To eliminate means to get rid of.

Trachoma is an eye disease caused by a germ, a bacterium. It spreads when people touch eye or nose goo from someone who has it. Getting it again and again scars the eyelid. Then the eyelashes turn inward, toward the eye. That can cause blindness.
WHO says trachoma is the world's leading infectious cause of blindness. Infectious means it spreads from person to person. It is linked to being poor and to not having clean water.

So how did Eritrea beat it? It followed a WHO plan called SAFE. S is for Surgery. A is for Antibiotics, medicines that kill bacteria. F is for Facial cleanliness, or clean faces. E is for Environmental improvement, such as clean water and toilets.

WHO's leader, Tedros, said the work took two decades, or 20 years. Eritrea is the 34th country in the world to beat trachoma. Worldwide, the number of people needing help with it fell by about 94 percent between 2002 and November 2025.

challenge.title: BE VOYAGER'S RADIO TEAM
body: Pretend one room is Earth and another room is Voyager 1. Earth writes a short question on paper. A messenger may only carry it after a kitchen timer counts one minute. Each minute stands for the 24 hours a real radio message now takes to reach the probe.

Now Voyager writes an answer, and the messenger waits another minute to carry it back. How long did Earth wait for its answer? Write the time down. Then swap jobs, so everyone gets a turn to be Earth, Voyager and the messenger.
Next, try a question that needs two answers in a row, such as a riddle with a clue. Count the minutes again. Each extra question adds two more minutes of waiting.
Talk about what you learned. When a reply takes two whole days, every question has to count. How would you write your question so Voyager only needs to answer once?

Bonus, be a meerkat: with a grown-up, walk a short way from your front door, in your yard or a park. Stand tall, look for landmarks you know, then point straight toward home. Were you right? The meerkats in the Kalahari got home in 18 of 20 tries.

Bonus, make a SAFE poster: fold a sheet of paper into four boxes. Write S, A, F and E, one in each box, and draw a picture for each part of WHO's plan. For F, draw someone washing their face with clean water.

did_you_know.text: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. In 1990, Voyager 1 turned its camera back toward home and took a famous photo called the Pale Blue Dot. In it, Earth looks like a tiny speck in a sunbeam. Voyager 1 also carries a Golden Record of sounds from Earth. NASA expects it to last more than a billion years.

explainer.title: HOW RADIO WAVES CROSS SPACE
body: Radio waves are a kind of light that our eyes cannot see. Like all light, they travel about 186,000 miles every second. They do not need air, so they can cross empty space.

Far away, a radio signal gets very weak. So NASA's Deep Space Network uses giant dish-shaped antennas. A dish gathers faint waves and bounces them to one spot, a bit like cupping a hand behind your ear. That is how engineers can still hear Voyager 1's carrier signal, a plain radio tone with no data in it.

Voyager 1 also needs power to send its signal. Its power comes from plutonium, a material that slowly gives off heat, which is turned into electricity. Each year the probe has about 4 watts less power, about what a small night-light uses. NASA expects its science instruments to keep working until at least its 50th launch birthday next summer.

A plain tone sounds useless, but it still helps. Engineers know Voyager 1's path through space very well. By putting the tone together with careful maths about that path, they confirmed it had reached one light-day.
Voyager 1 still zooms along at about 38,000 miles an hour. A car on a highway goes about 60.
